name_en: Liu An Lan Cha (Anhui Basket Tea)
cultivar: Qimen small-leaf population bushes (the same stock as Keemun)
processing: Basket-matured dark tea made in stages: spring leaf is withered, fixed, rolled and dried into raw tea and stored through the summer; around Bailu in early autumn it is sorted, blended and fired, spread outdoors for one night to take the dew and regain moisture, then steamed, wrapped in ruoye bamboo leaves, packed into bamboo baskets, dried a final time and stored to mature.
harvest_season: Spring, beginning around Guyu in late April; the raw tea rests through summer and is finished and basketed around Bailu in early autumn.
appearance_dry: Lightly matted dark-brown leaf in a small bamboo basket, lined and topped with dried ruoye bamboo leaves.
appearance_liquor: Amber to orange-red, clear, darkening with age.
appearance_wet: Small, even dark-brown leaves, tender for a dark tea.
taste_profile: Mild, sweet and smooth with bamboo leaf, a light betel-nut woodiness and a faint herbal, medicinal note; aged baskets gain depth and a cooling finish.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, boiling water, short steeps; drop a piece of the bamboo-leaf lining into the pot, as the Guangdong tea houses do. Young baskets are better simmered briefly.

vintage_note: Sold by the year the basket was made, usually as whole baskets and sometimes repacked loose, from the current year to old lots. Young baskets are a little green and astringent and usually rested for some years. Baskets said to date from the 1980s and 90s revival under the Sun Yi Shun name are collectables, and their dates are hard to prove.
description:
Liu An Lan Cha, now officially Qimen An Cha, is Anhui's basket-matured dark tea, and it has a geography problem: it shares a name with Lu'an, the place in western Anhui, but it is made around Luxi in southern Qimen County, the home of Keemun. How the name attached to it is unresolved. It was long a tea of Guangdong, Hong Kong and Southeast Asia, carried south in small bamboo baskets and sold through tea and medicine shops, with some physicians using it as a medicinal carrier. Sun Yi Shun is the old brand name that survives from that trade; regular production had largely stopped by the end of the war with Japan and was revived from the 1980s, after a Hong Kong merchant asked for it.

It is made quite differently from the Hunan and Guangxi teas. Spring leaf is fixed, rolled and dried into raw tea and rested through the summer. Around Bailu in early autumn it is sorted and fired, left out for one night to take the dew, which makers say gives the leaf back the moisture it needs for steaming, then steamed, packed into small bamboo baskets lined with ruoye leaves and dried again before it is put away to mature. There is no big pile and no smoke, which is why it stays light and clean, closer in spirit to a gently aged tea than to a brick.

In the cup it is mild, sweet and smooth with bamboo leaf, a light betel-nut woodiness and a faint herbal note; aged baskets deepen and pick up a cooling, medicinal finish without losing their gentleness. Brew it with boiling water after a rinse and it gives many steeps; a piece of the bamboo-leaf lining in the pot is traditional and adds to the flavour. Young baskets can be a touch green and astringent and are better after a few years or simmered briefly.

It is sold by basket year by a few Qimen makers and through Hong Kong and Guangdong dealers; the Sun Yi Shun name is the historic one and the one most imitated. Later Hong Kong teas sold as Liu An can be made from quite different material, so ask where a basket was made. Look for an intact basket with a clean, sweet, bamboo smell; the tea should be dry and springy, not damp. Old baskets command high prices on the strength of the name, and the cup, not the label, is the only check on them.

If you like Liu Bao but want something lighter and more delicate, this is the tea; if you drink Keemun, it is another life of the same county's hills.
sources_note: The night-dew ('ye lu') step and the gentle basket firing follow Chinese descriptions of the traditional method; the 1980s revival and the Sun Yi Shun brand history are from trade accounts. 'Lu'an' is the standard reading of 六安, though 'Liu An' is common in tea-shop usage.
history:
This dark tea carries two names and a puzzle. Today it is officially Qimen An Cha, made around Luxi in southern Qimen County, yet for much of the twentieth century buyers in Guangdong, Hong Kong and Southeast Asia knew it as Liu An, a name now tied to a different green tea from western Anhui. Why it took that name is unresolved. One press account says Qimen merchants first imitated Liu An tea in the late Ming or early Qing, and a surviving Sun Yi Shun tea ticket links Liu An with a sales house in Foshan, but neither settles the question.

The trade ran south through Jiangxi to Foshan and Hong Kong. A 1932 register, known only through later transcriptions, lists 47 firms, and a 1941 book reports about 3,000 dan a year sold to Guangdong and Guangxi, with physicians in eastern Guangdong using it as a medicinal carrier. War broke the route, and regular production had largely stopped by its end.

The revival began with a letter. In 1983 Hong Kong merchant Guan Fenfa sent an aged basket to the Anhui Provincial Tea Company asking whether the tea could be made again. Technicians went to the Luxi villages the next year, studied old baskets and talked to retired makers. Accounts differ on exactly when production resumed, and it took several years.
